'''Corfe Castle''' is a fortification standing above [[Corfe Castle (village)|the village of the same name]] on the [[Isle of Purbeck]] peninsula in the English county of [[Dorset]]. Built by [[William the Conqueror]], the castle dates to the 11th century and commands a gap in the [[Purbeck Hills]] on the route between [[Wareham, Dorset|Wareham]] and [[Swanage]]. The first phase was one of the earliest castles in England to be built at least partly using stone when the majority were built with earth and timber. Corfe Castle underwent major structural changes in the 12th and 13th centuries.

In 1572, Corfe Castle left the Crown's control when [[Elizabeth I]] sold it to Sir [[Christopher Hatton]]. Sir [[John Bankes]] bought the castle in 1635, and was the owner during the [[English Civil War]]. While Bankes was fighting in London and Oxford, his wife, Lady [[Mary Bankes]], led the defence of the castle when it was twice besieged by [[Roundhead|Parliamentarian forces]]. The first siege, in 1643, was unsuccessful, but by 1645 Corfe was one of the last remaining [[cavalier|royalist]] strongholds in southern England and fell to a siege ending in an assault. In March that year Corfe Castle was [[slighting|slighted]] on Parliament's orders. Owned by the [[National Trust]], the castle is open to the public and in 2018 received around 237,000 visitors.<ref name="ALVA 2018 visitor numbers">{{cite web|title=ALVA - Association of Leading Visitor Attractions|url=http://www.alva.org.uk/details.cfm?p=423|website=www.alva.org.uk|access-date=25 August 2019}}</ref> It is protected as a grade I [[listed building]]<ref>{{cite web|title=CORFE CASTLE, Corfe Castle - 1121000 {{!}} Historic England|url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1121000|access-date=30 May 2022|website=historicengland.org.uk}}</ref> and a [[scheduled monument]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Corfe Castle: a large enclosure castle, and 18th century Vineyard Bridge, Corfe Castle - 1011487 {{!}} Historic England|url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1011487|access-date=30 May 2022|website=historicengland.org.uk}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:Corfe Castle 1856 OS map.png|thumb|upright=1.2|[[Ordnance Survey]] map of Corfe Castle in 1856, showing the castle and village in the gap of the [[Purbeck Hills]]]]

===Royal castle===
Corfe Castle was built on a steep hill in a gap in a long line of chalk hills, created by two streams eroding the rock on either side. The name ''Corfe'' derives from the [[Old English]] {{lang|ang|ceorfan}}, meaning 'a cutting', referring to the gap.<ref>{{cite book|title=Dorset Villages|last=Gant|first=Roland|publisher=Robert Hale |page=214|year=1980|isbn=0-7091-8135-3}}</ref> The construction of the medieval castle means that little is known about previous activity on the hill. We know from contemporary writing that Anglo-Saxon nobility treated it as a residence, such as Queen [[Ælfthryth, wife of Edgar]], and there are [[posthole]]s belonging to a Saxon hall on the site.<ref>{{harvnb|Yarrow|2005|p=4}}.</ref> This hall may be where the boy-king [[Edward the Martyr]] was assassinated in 978, possibly aged sixteen; contemporaries tell us that he went to the castle at Corfe to visit Ælfthryth and his brother.<ref>{{harvnb|Royal Commission on Historic Monuments (England)|1970|p=57}}.</ref>

A castle was founded at Corfe on England's south coast soon after the [[Norman conquest of England]] in 1066. The [[royal forest]] of [[Isle of Purbeck|Purbeck]], where [[William the Conqueror]] enjoyed hunting, was established in the area.<ref name=Yarrow7>{{harvnb|Yarrow|2005|p=7}}.</ref> Between 1066 and 1087, William established 36 such castles in England.<ref>{{harvnb|Liddiard|2005|p=18}}.</ref> The castle stood {{cvt|21|m}} tall atop a {{cvt|55|m}} high hill.<ref>{{cite web|title=The history of Corfe Castle|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/dorset/corfe-castle/the-history-of-corfe-castle|publisher=National Trust|access-date=19 October 2024}}</ref> Sitting as it does on a hill top, Corfe Castle is one of the classic images of a medieval castle. However, despite popular imagination, occupying the highest point in the landscape was not the typical position of a medieval castle. In England, a minority are located on hilltops, but most are in valleys; many were near important transport routes such as river crossings.<ref>{{harvnb|Liddiard|2005|p=24}}.</ref>

Unusually for castles built in the 11th century, Corfe was partially constructed from stone indicating it was of particularly high status. A stone wall was built around the hill top, creating an inner ward or enclosure. There were two further enclosures: one to the west, and one that extended south (the outer bailey); in contrast to the inner bailey, these were surrounded by [[palisade]]s made from timber.<ref name=Yarrow7/> At the time, the vast majority of castles in England were built using earth and timber, and it was not until the 12th century that many began to be rebuilt in stone.<ref>{{harvnb|King|1988|p=62}}.</ref> The [[Domesday Book]] of 1086 records one castle in Dorset; the entry, which reads "Of the manor of Kingston the King has one hide on which he built Wareham castle", is thought to refer to Corfe rather than the timber castle at [[Wareham, Dorset|Wareham]].<ref>{{harvnb|Harfield|1991|p=376}}.</ref> There are 48 castles directly mentioned in the Domesday Book, although not all those in existence at the time were recorded.<ref>{{harvnb|Harfield|1991|pp=384, 388}}.</ref> Assuming that Corfe is the castle in question, it is one of four the Domesday Book attributes to William the Conqueror; the survey explicitly mentions seven people as having built castles, of whom William was the most prolific.<ref>{{harvnb|Harfield|1991|p=391}}.</ref>

[[File:Corfe Castle before its destruction - geograph.org.uk - 1506230.jpg|thumb|A model of Corfe Castle before its destruction]]
[[File:Corfe Castle sunlit - geograph.org.uk - 456603.jpg|thumb|View of Corfe Castle from West Hill]]

In the early 12th century, [[Henry I of England|Henry I]] began the construction of a stone [[keep]] at Corfe. Progressing at a rate of {{convert|3|to|4|m|0}} per year for the best part of a decade, the work began in around 1096 or 1097 and was complete by 1105. The chalk of the hill Corfe Castle was built on was an unsuitable building material, and instead [[Purbeck limestone]] quarried a few miles away was used.<ref>{{harvnb|Yarrow|2005|pp=7–8}}.</ref> By the reign of King [[Stephen, King of England|Stephen]] (1135–1154) Corfe Castle was already a strong fortress with a keep and inner enclosure, both built in stone.<ref>{{harvnb|Royal Commission on Historic Monuments (England)|1970|p=59}}.</ref> In 1139, during the [[The Anarchy|civil war]] of Stephen's reign, Corfe withstood a siege by the King.<ref name=RCHME60>{{harvnb|Royal Commission on Historic Monuments (England)|1970|p=60}}.</ref> It is thought that he built a [[siege castle]] to facilitate the siege and that a series of earthworks about {{convert|290|m|yd|-1}} south-southwest of Corfe Castle mark the site of the fortification.<ref name="the rings">{{citation|url=https://www.heritagegateway.org.uk/Gateway/Results_Single.aspx?uid=456823&resourceID=19191|title=The Rings|publisher=English Heritage|work=Pastscape|access-date=19 October 2024}}</ref>

[[File:Corfe Castle Gatetower and Bridge.jpg|thumb|The south-west gatehouse, which allowed access from the outer bailey to the west bailey, dates from the mid 13th century. The masonry is of high quality.]]
During the reign of [[Henry II of England|Henry II]] Corfe Castle was probably not significantly changed, and records from [[Richard I of England|Richard]]'s reign indicate maintenance rather than significant new building work.<ref name=RCHME60/> In contrast, extensive construction of other towers, halls and walls occurred during the reigns of [[John, King of England|John]] and [[Henry III of England|Henry III]], both of whom kept [[Eleanor, Fair Maid of Brittany|Eleanor, rightful Duchess of Brittany]] who posed a potential threat to their crowns, in confinement at Corfe until 1222. John also kept Scottish hostages [[Margaret of Scotland, Countess of Kent|Margaret of Scotland]] and [[Isabella of Scotland, Countess of Norfolk|Isabella of Scotland]] there. In 1203, [[Savari de Mauléon]] was also imprisoned, but reputedly escaped by getting his jailers drunk and then overpowering them.<ref>{{cite book|title=The Plantagenets|last=Harvey|first=John|publisher=B. T. Batsford|year=1948}}</ref> It was probably during John's reign that the [[Gloriette]] in the [[inner bailey]] was built. The [[Pipe Rolls]], records of royal expenditure, show that between 1201 and 1204 over £750 was spent at the castle, probably on rebuilding the defences of the west bailey with £275 spent on constructing the Gloriette.<ref name=RCHME60/> The [[Royal Commission on the Historical Monuments of England]] noted the link between periods of unrest and building at Corfe. In the early years of his reign, John lost [[Duchy of Normandy|Normandy]] to the French, and further building work at Corfe coincided with the political disturbances later in his reign. At least £500 was spent between 1212 and 1214 and may have been focused on the defences of the outer bailey.<ref name="Royal Commission on Historic Monuments England 1970 61">{{harvnb|Royal Commission on Historic Monuments (England)|1970|p=61}}.</ref> R. Allen Brown noted that in John's reign "it would seem
that though a fortress of the first order might cost more than £7,000, a medium castle of reasonable strength might be built for less than £2,000".<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|1955|p=366}}.</ref> The Pipe Rolls show that John spent over £17,000 on 95 castles during his reign spread; he spent over £500 at nine of them, of which Corfe was one. Additional records show that John spent over £1,400 at Corfe Castle.<ref>{{harvnb|Brown|1955|pp=356, 368}}.</ref>

One of the secondary roles of castles was to act as a storage facility, as demonstrated by Corfe Castle; in 1224 [[Henry III of England|Henry III]] sent to Corfe for 15,000 crossbow bolts to be used in the siege of [[Bedford Castle]]. Following John's work, Henry III also spent over £1,000 on Corfe Castle, in particular the years 1235 and 1236 saw £362 spent on the keep.<ref name="Royal Commission on Historic Monuments England 1970 61"/><ref>{{harvnb|Brown|1976|pp=148–149}}.</ref> While construction was under-way, a camp to accommodate the workers was established outside the castle. Over time, this grew into a settlement in its own right and in 1247 was granted a market and fair by royal permission.<ref>{{harvnb|Yarrow|2005|p=14}}.</ref> It was Henry III who ordered in 1244 that Corfe's keep should be whitewashed.<ref>{{harvnb|Yarrow|2005|p=9}}.</ref> Four years previously, he also ordered that the keep of the [[Tower of London]] should be whitewashed, and it therefore became known as the [[White Tower (Tower of London)|White Tower]].<ref>{{harvnb|Impey|Parnell|2000|pp=25–27}}.</ref>

[[Michael de la Pole, 1st Earl of Suffolk]], was kept imprisoned at Corfe for a few weeks in November 1386 after being impeached by the [[Wonderful Parliament]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Saul|first=Nigel|title=Richard II|year=2008|page=159|publisher=Yale University Press|location=New Haven, Connecticut|isbn=978-0300078756}}</ref> On 10 December 1450, Corfe was ransacked by the tenants of [[Richard of York, 3rd Duke of York]], as the castle had served as the chief residence for his political rival, [[Edmund Beaufort, 2nd Duke of Somerset]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Jones|first=Michael K.|title=Somerset, York and the Wars of the Roses|journal=[[The English Historical Review]]|date=April 1989|volume=104|issue=411|page=288|jstor=571736}}</ref>

In December 1460, during the [[Wars of the Roses]] Henry Beaufort and his army marched from the castle destined for the [[Battle of Wakefield]]. During the march the army split at [[Exeter]] so the cavalry could reach the north quicker, and on 16 December 1460 some of his men became embroiled in the [[Battle of Worksop]] in [[Nottinghamshire]]. Beaufort and the Lancastrians won the skirmish.

===After the medieval period===
{{See also|Dorset in the English Civil War}}
The castle remained a royal fortress until sold by [[Elizabeth I]] in 1572 to her [[Lord Chancellor]], Sir [[Christopher Hatton]]. Ralph Treswell, Hatton's steward, drafted a series of plans of the castle; the documents are the oldest surviving survey of the castle.<ref>{{harvnb|Yarrow|2005|p=24}}.</ref>

[[File:Mary Bankes-Hawtry by Henry Pierce Bone, after John Hoskins.jpg|thumb|upright=0.75|Lady [[Mary Bankes]] defended the castle during two sieges in the English Civil War.]]
The castle was bought by Sir [[John Bankes]], [[Attorney General for England and Wales|Attorney General]] to [[Charles I of England|Charles I]], in 1635.<ref>{{harvnb|Brooks|2004}}.</ref> The [[English Civil War]] broke out in 1642, and by 1643 most of Dorset was under [[Roundhead|Parliamentarian]] control. While Bankes was in Oxford with the King, his men held Corfe Castle in the royal cause. During this time his wife, [[Mary, Lady Bankes]], resided at the castle with their children. Parliamentarian forces planned to infiltrate the castle's garrison by joining a hunting party from the garrison on a [[May Day]] hunt; however they were unsuccessful. The Parliamentarians gave orders that anyone joining the garrison would have their house burned and that no supplies were to reach the castle. Initially defended by just five people, Lady Bankes was able to get food through and swell the garrison to 80. The Parliamentarian forces numbered between 500 and 600 and began a more thorough siege; it went on for six weeks until Lady Bankes was relieved by [[Cavalier|Royalist]] forces. During the siege the defenders suffered two casualties while there were at least 100 deaths among the besieging force.<ref>{{harvnb|Yarrow|2005|p=26}}.</ref>

[[File:Corfe Castle Ruins, Dorset - geograph.org.uk - 1492352.jpg|thumb|left|In the 17th century Corfe Castle was [[slighted]] by order of parliament.]]
The Parliamentarians were in the ascendency so that by 1645 Corfe Castle was one of a few remaining strongholds in southern England that remained under royal control. Consequently, it was besieged by a force under the command of [[John Bingham (Roundhead)|Colonel Bingham]]. One of the royalist garrison's officers, Colonel Pitman, colluded with Bingham. Pitman proposed to Bankes that he should go to Somerset and bring back a hundred royalist men as reinforcements; however the troops he returned with were Parliamentarians in disguise. Once inside, they waited until the besieging force attacked before making a move, so that the defenders were attacked from without and within at the same time. Corfe Castle was captured and Lady Bankes and the garrison were allowed to leave. In March that year, the town of [[Poole]] petitioned Parliament to demolish the Castle and to allocate the proceeds and any fines levied on Lady Bankes for the "relief and Maintenance of the Soldiers and poor Inhabitants of the said Town of Poole, and other Garrisons of that County", that had been loyal to Parliament.<ref>{{cite journal|title=House of Lords Journal|date=18 October 1645|journal=Journal of the House of Lords|volume=7|orig-date=1644|publisher=His Majesty's Stationery Office|location=London|url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/lords-jrnl/vol7/pp647-648#h3-0015|pages=647–648}}</ref> Parliament voted to [[Slighting|slight]] (demolish) the castle, giving it its present appearance.<ref>{{harvnb|Yarrow|2005|pp=26–28}}.</ref> In the 17th century many castles in England were obsolete and in a state of decline, but the war saw them pressed into use as fortresses one more time. Parliament ordered the slighting of many of these fortifications, but the solidity of their walls meant that complete demolition was often impracticable. A minority were repaired after the war, but most were left as ruins. Corfe Castle provided a ready supply of building material, and its stones were reused by the villagers.<ref>{{harvnb|Cantor|1987|pp=93–94}}.</ref>

After [[English Restoration|the restoration]] of the monarchy in 1660, the [[Bankes family]] regained their properties. Rather than rebuild or replace the ruined castle they chose to build a new house at [[Kingston Lacy]] on their other Dorset estate near [[Wimborne Minster]].

The first [[Excavation (archaeology)|archaeological excavations]] were carried out in 1883. No further archaeological work was carried out on the site until the 1950s. Between 1986 and 1997 excavations were carried out, jointly funded by the National Trust and [[English Heritage]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pastscape.org.uk/monumentinfo.aspx?a=0&hob_id=456826|title=Corfe Castle, Dorset: Excavation History|publisher=English Heritage|work=Pastscape|access-date=5 January 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121023190918/http://www.pastscape.org.uk/monumentinfo.aspx?a=0&hob_id=456826|archive-date=23 October 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref> Corfe Castle is considered to be the inspiration for [[Enid Blyton]]'s [[The Famous Five (novel series)|Kirrin Island]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.enidblyton.net/famous-five/create-your-very-own-kirrin-island.html|title=Create Your Very Own Kirrin Island|first=Keith |last=Robinson|website=Enid Blyton.net|access-date=9 January 2012}}</ref> which had its own similar castle. It was used as a shooting location for the 1957 film series ''[[Five on a Treasure Island (film)|Five on a Treasure Island]]'' and the 1971 film ''[[Bedknobs and Broomsticks]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.south-central-media.co.uk/purbeck/purbeck.htm|title=The Isle of Purbeck On Screen|website=South Central MediaScene|access-date=17 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305055518/http://www.south-central-media.co.uk/purbeck/purbeck.htm|archive-date=5 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> The castle plays an important part in [[Keith Roberts]]' [[uchronia]] novel ''[[Pavane (novel)|Pavane]]''.

{{wideimage|Corfe Castle stitch 1.jpg|1000px|Corfe Castle is on a hill overlooking the village which bears its name.}}

==Current status==
[[File:Corfe Castle, Entrance - geograph.org.uk - 1722689.jpg|thumb|Corfe Castle's outer gatehouse]]
[[File:Corfe Castle - geograph.org.uk - 1005257.jpg|left|thumb|Corfe Castle in 1980 before the bequest of the castle to the [[National Trust]], and its subsequent restoration]]

Upon his death, [[Ralph Bankes (landowner)|Ralph Bankes]] (1902–1981) bequeathed the entire Bankes estate to the [[National Trust]], including Corfe Castle, much of the village of Corfe, the family home at [[Kingston Lacy]], and substantial property and land holdings elsewhere in the area.

In mid-2006, the dangerous condition of the keep caused it to be closed to visitors, who could only visit the walls and inner bailey. The National Trust undertook an extensive conservation project on the castle, and the keep was re-opened to visitors in 2008, and the work completed the following year.<ref>{{cite web|title=Corfe Castle|work=historicengland.org.uk|url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1121000|access-date=18 August 2006}}</ref><ref>National Trust Annual Report 2004-05.</ref> During the restoration work, an "appearance" door was found in the keep, designed for Henry I.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bournemouthecho.co.uk/news/2347529.secret_perch_of_a_pious_pelican/|title=Secret perch of a pious pelican|work=[[Bournemouth Daily Echo]]|date=18 June 2008|access-date=19 October 2024|last=Smith|first=Steven}}</ref> The National Trust claims that this indicates that the castle would have been one of the most important in England at the time.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/2008/jun/18/heritage.archaeology|title=Find points to high status of castle|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|date=18 June 2008|access-date=19 October 2024|last=Morris|first=Steven}}</ref>

==Layout==
[[File:Corfe plan 1586.png|thumb|upright=1.2|A plan of Corfe Castle from 1586, drawn up by Ralph Treswell]]
Corfe Castle is roughly triangular and divided into three parts, known as enclosures or wards.<ref>{{harvnb|Royal Commission on Historic Monuments (England)|1970|p=58}}.</ref>

Enclosed in the 11th century, the inner ward contained the castle's [[keep]], also known as a donjon or great tower, which was built partly on the enclosure's curtain wall. It is uncertain when the keep was built though dates of around 1100–1130 have been suggested, placing it within the reign of Henry I. Attached to the keep's west face is a forebuilding containing a stair through which the great tower was entered. On the south side is an extension with a guardroom and a chapel. The two attachments postdate the construction of the keep itself, but were built soon after. To the east of the keep within the inner ward is a building known as the [[gloriette]]. Only ruins are left of the gloriette which was probably built by King John.<ref>{{harvnb|Royal Commission on Historic Monuments (England)|1970|pp=59–60}}.</ref>

The remains of the west bailey, the stone wall with three towers, date from 1202 to 1204 when it was refortified.<ref name=RCHME60/> It resembles the bailey of [[Château Gaillard]] in [[Normandy]], France, built for [[Richard I of England|Richard I]] in 1198.<ref>{{harvnb|Royal Commission on Historical Monuments (England)|1960|p=36}}.</ref>
